title: I gathered one of the largest social media sentiment datasets available to retail investors and wrapped it in an MCP. Have you ever wondered what other investors are thinking?
author: rumor_io
selftext:
I built [Rumor.io](https://rumor.io/). Connect Rumor with an AI assistant and ask it questions like

*Which Apple keynote over the past 10 years was the most popular?*

*Which stock have investors lost faith in?*

*Which ticker has the most committed fans?*

[Rumor.io](https://rumor.io/) tracks 14k+ stocks, cryptocurrencies and ETFs across 1.5 billion posts with a 15+ year history. It combines one of the largest datasets with fundamentals and a news API.  
  
Why should investors care about social media sentiment? 

Benjamin Graham famously said "in the short run, the market is a voting machine, but in the long run, it is a weighing machine."

Well, how do you measure the voting machine? 

In Burton Malkiel's *A Random Walk Down Wall Street.* He describes two theories of asset valuation, the **Firm-Foundation Theory** and the **Castle-in-the-Air Theory.**

You're probably familiar with the **Firm-Foundation Theory**, it claims that every investment has a true intrinsic value based on future cash flows, earnings, and dividends.

The **Castle-in-the-Air** theory is all about crowd psychology. It believes investments have value because other people believe they have value. It describes cryptocurrencies, meme stocks and sets the price for Chanel bags. It's hype, newsprint, and stock tips from your hair dresser.

It was always possible to measure the **Firm-Foundation**, but we've only recently been able to measure the **Castle-in-the-Air** with the ubiquity of social media.

I built Rumor to join the **Firm-Foundation** AND the **Castle-in-the-Air**.

Choose investments with a firm foundation that also have the attention of the crowd. Try to understand what appeals to investors. It doesn't mean always following the hype, it's about anticipating where the hype is going next.

>“The key to success is being where other investors will be, several months before they get there. So ask yourself whether the story about your stock is one that is likely to catch the fancy of the crowd. Can the story generate contagious dreams? Is it a story on which investors can build castles in the air—but castles in the air that really rest on a firm foundation?” — Burton Malkiel

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: the thing I'd want to know before trusting a backtest on it is whether the history is point in time. deleted posts, suspended accounts and delisted tickers all vanish from a scrape done today, and the sentiment that's left looks smarter than it was in the moment.

replies.author: rumor_io
replies.body:
Yes, I agree this is a hard problem. Another issue: it's probably impossible to know exactly how much engagement a post had at the time, and our metrics are engagement-weighted.

It's an extremely fun dataset to study, though. We have more hypotheses than time to test them. For example, around earnings: the tone of the posts doesn't predict a beat or a miss, but a buildup in how much people are talking about a stock beforehand does say something about how big the move will be.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: A 15-year history across that many posts is a serious dataset. The key question for investors is lead versus lag: does sentiment move before price, or just follow it? That depends on whether post timestamps are first-seen, how bots and deleted posts are handled, and whether it's point-in-time, so a backtest can't see a post before it existed. Splitting sentiment around scheduled events could also help, and Cymetica's EventTrader is one source of earnings and macro timing for that.
